decisions.what: Kept the builder's out-of-scope deletion of J-5's prose allowlist, but did NOT accept its stated rationale
decisions.why: The builder called the allowlist a live silent hole. Measured both arms myself: a FALSE prose count fires on both trees; a TRUE prose count is SILENT on the unfixed tree and FIRES on the fixed one. So the allowlist was not permitting unverified counts while the prose readers lived — it went dead when they were retired, and the deletion converts the section to the Attribution section's existing C7 policy (counts in tables, no digits in prose). Defensible and kept; the justification as written overstated the case, and the real cost — an honest TRUE restatement in prose is now refused — is recorded rather than buried.

decisions.what: Cited run 32400996331 at commit 4b63e91, NOT the newer run 32401050374 at 2014bb9
decisions.why: The README section states its own selection rule — 'the most recent full matrix run against a commit that actually changed src/, bin/, test/, or the workflow itself'. 2014bb9 is more recent and its run is green, but it touched only .swarm/, so it is ineligible under the section's own words. Citing the newest green run would have satisfied the machine guard (the diff would still be empty) while violating the prose rule the guard exists to serve — green bought by reading the check instead of the claim. The builder derived this independently and rejected 2014bb9 for the same reason.

decisions.why: The rows describe a REMOTE run (32400996331 @ 4b63e91) that really did report 124/122/0/2. decisions.what: Corrected KI-R6-6's diagnosis mid-WRAP_UP after reading the pacer log, having already written the wrong version into state.json, REPORT.md, RETRO.md and the playbook
decisions.why: The first diagnosis was inferred from the SHAPE of the evidence — a 25.5h gap with no commits, plus a known-dead watchdog — and it named the pacer as the thing that failed. Reading /opt/swarm/runs/pacer.log falsified it in one command: 504 spawns, 503 completions, every one a 429 weekly-limit. The wrong version was not merely imprecise, it pointed at the wrong fix: a pacer liveness check would have passed every time while the run stayed dead. This is the same error class this run spent five cycles hunting in documents — a claim restated confidently from adjacent evidence instead of measured at its source — committed by the conductor, in the write-up, about its own harness. Corrected in all five artifacts rather than left standing with a footnote.

The README Node-support matrix can still be falsified WHOLESALE: gate cell C7 (cycle 4) changed all four rows together to a self-consistent falsehood (200 tests, 198 pass, 0 fail, 2 skipped) and test/readme-matrix-consistency.test.js stayed SILENT at 5 pass / 0 fail. Per-row arithmetic and cross-row agreement catch a single bad row, a transcription slip, or a partial edit — not a lie told consistently. Closing it requires an anchor outside the document (live network provenance, which would skip in the shallow-CI environment the table describes; or a committed machine-readable CI artifact, which changes what CI is responsible for). docs/node-support-citation-history.md PARAPHRASES the rewritten citation-selection rule instead of quoting the README's wording, and the paraphrase is a different rule: it selects 'the most recent run whose cited commit's src/bin/test/.github content is byte-identical to this tree', which on this tree selects 3a5d6e3 @ run 32405575919 (more recent, and `git diff 7e50d6f..3a5d6e3 -- src bin test .github` is empty) — NOT the 7e50d6f the README cites. The README's own rule ('the matrix run for the push that carried the last change to those paths') selects 7e50d6f uniquely and is correct. No guard reads the history file's prose, so nothing catches the disagreement. Fix is one line: quote the README's rule verbatim instead of restating it. Q-10.

The run overshot stop_at by 25.5h — and the FIRST diagnosis of why, written earlier this same cycle, was WRONG and is corrected here. It said 'the pacer produced no cycle'. The pacer log says otherwise: between 2026-08-20T18:59:48Z and 2026-08-22T16:04:02Z it fired faithfully every ~5 minutes and SPAWNED 504 cycles. 503 of them completed; ALL 503 died in ~380ms with HTTP 429, `You've hit your weekly limit · resets Aug 24, 5am (UTC)`, before their first turn. Zero other failure causes — the classification is exhaustive, not a sample. This is precisely L-037's FIRST clause re-observed: a spawned conductor that dies on a usage-limit error before its first turn is invisible to limp mode, because limp needs a session alive enough to run the tier probe, so the SPAWNER must set the limp flag itself on a usage-shaped launch failure instead of respawning on the same schedule. It does not: swarm-pacer.sh logs `cycle-failed` and retries at the same cadence, burning 504 spawns against a wall. The runfile's own last probe had already recorded weekly_used_pct: 100. Human item, and note the correction cost: a liveness check on the pacer (the fix the wrong diagnosis implied) would have PASSED throughout — the pacer was alive; what was dead was every session it started.
